extracted.intended_audience: poets, writers, and aspiring authors (especially those seeking patronage)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and moral guidance for poets and literary men about composing, publishing, and managing relationships with patrons and the public; includes conduct, stylistic, and career advice. Drawn from Horace's epistles, aimed at producing durable, respectable work and securing favorable reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit patronage with modesty and caution
rubrics_metrics.description: The friendship of great men is a laudable acquisition, yet their favors are ever to be solicited with modesty and caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not loudly proclaim poverty or press importunately for favors; modestly accepting or waiting often gains more than clamorous begging. Examples/anti-patterns: the man who cries out about his sister's want or pleads publicly fares worse than the one who keeps silent and discreet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer an active/business life over private inactivity
rubrics_metrics.description: That a life of business is preferable to a private and inactive one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in useful affairs rather than retreat into idleness; activity brings honor and opportunity (and makes one fit to claim reward for exploits), whereas inactivity is unbecoming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep complaints and needs discreet before superiors
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who mention nothing of their poverty before their lord, will gain more than the importunate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly lamenting hardships or repeating petty complaints undermines credibility (example: companion constantly weeping about stolen provisions loses all credit). Silence or modest appeal is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frequent lamentation and theatrical grief
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent tears and repeated lamentations cause others to withhold belief in your real grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to a harlot who weeps so often for lost trinkets that real grief is ignored. Anti-pattern: habitual dramatics that desensitize spectators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yield to a friend's tastes in company (practical deference)
rubrics_metrics.description: When your friend in power leads his dogs to the field or enjoys his amusements, arise and lay aside peevishness of your unmannerly muse that you may sup together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt your behavior and entertainments to those of your patron when in his company; avoid behaving so as to offend or appear intractable—practical deference secures favor and conviviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obsequious flattery and maintain balanced sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of imitating a flatterer; virtue is the medium between flattery and bluntness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be a 'toad-eater' who slavishly repeats a superior's words; nor be crude bluntness that offends. Aim for honest, measured speech—neither servile nor churlish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep confidences; do not pry or gossip
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not at any time pry into his secrets; keep close what is intrusted to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inquisitive impertinence and tattling; a word once sent abroad 'flies irrevocably.' Even under wine or passion, maintain discretion. Anti-pattern: loose talkers whose open ears fail to retain confidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet people you recommend carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Look over and over again into the merits of such a one, as you recommend; lest afterward the faults of others strike you with shame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoroughly examine the character and abilities of those you endorse; once deceived, do not defend the self-inflicted faults of the unworthy—protect and patronize only those known to you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend a patron's levee with caution and maintain your own work
rubrics_metrics.description: The attending of the levee of a friend in power seems delightful to the unexperienced; the experienced dreads it. Do you, while your vessel is in the main, ply your business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of being drawn away from your own obligations by courtly life; continue to 'ply your business' and avoid being stranded by changing gales of favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and consult the learned to cultivate a calm, agreeable life
rubrics_metrics.description: In every thing you must read and consult the learned, by what means you may be enabled to pass your life in an agreeable manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study what truly lessens cares and leads to equanimity—learn whether virtue or nature produces calm; use learning to moderate desire and attain inner peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid slavish imitation; seek originality
rubrics_metrics.description: O ye imitators, ye servile herd, how often your bustlings have stirred my bile... I was the original, who set my free footsteps upon the vacant sod; I trod not in the steps of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not copy others' outward manner or subjects slavishly; imitation of faults deceives. Strive for originality in subject and style even if inspired by prior meters or forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not court the inconstant public's applause at art's expense
rubrics_metrics.description: I hunt not after the applause of the inconstant vulgar, at the expense of entertainments... I am not an auditor of noble writers, nor a vindictive reciter, nor condescend to court the tribes and desks of the grammarians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pandering to fickle audiences or sacrificing quality for immediate applause; be cautious of writing merely to please the mob or to chase spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject matter to your strength and capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither does your majesty admit of humble poetry, nor dares my modesty attempt a subject which my strength is unable to support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects within your capability; undertake great themes only if you possess the force to sustain them. Modesty in choosing scope preserves artistic credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize poetry's social functions: instruct, comfort, record virtue, and propitiate gods
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet fashions the child's tender and lisping mouth... he records virtuous actions, he instructs the rising age with approved examples, he comforts the indigent and the sick... With song the gods above are appeased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with awareness that poetry instructs morals, comforts communities, preserves exemplary deeds, and performs ritual/societal roles; aim to contribute these social goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not underestimate the labour of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is believed to require the least pains... but the less indulgence it meets with, the more labor it requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although comedy draws from common life, it still demands careful workmanship: crafting characters, comic timing, and stagecraft is hard work despite appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting work while fatigued, pained, or emotionally unsettled
rubrics_metrics.description: We poets... often do ourselves many mischiefs, when we present a work to you while thoughtful or fatigued; when we are pained, if my friend has dared to find fault with one line... when we lament that our labors do not appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from submitting or performing work when mentally or physically compromised; such presentations risk poor reception and self-inflicted harm. Do not re-read or re-present already repeated passages obsessively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be officious or overzealous in self-promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Yet officiousness foolishly disgusts the person whom it loves; especially when it recommends itself by numbers, and the art [of writing].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive zeal in promoting oneself or one's work alienates patrons; prefer modest, well-timed offers over pushy display. Anti-pattern: presenting poorly composed verses out of excessive zeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider publication consequences: books once released may be mistreated
rubrics_metrics.description: You seem, my book, to look wistfully at Janus and Vertumnus... There will be no returning for you, when you are once sent out... when thumbed by the hands of the vulgar, you begin to grow dirty; either you shall in silence feed the grovelling book-worms, or you shall make your escape to Utica...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious before publishing: a book goes into the public sphere and may be handled crudely, misused, or abused. Publish when ready and accept that public reception can be uncontrollable and degrading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize a well-ordered life over relentless composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The well-ordering of life is of more importance than the composition of verses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain balance between life and art; do not allow verse-writing to displace obligations or sound living. Honesty about personal limits and duties is preferable to overcommitment to publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live simply and avoid covetousness to preserve freedom and poetic character
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's mind is not easily covetous; fond of verses, he studies this alone; he laughs at losses, flights of slaves, fires; he contrives no fraud... he lives on husks, and brown bread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A modest lifestyle frees the poet from anxieties that corrupt character and craft. Covetousness breeds addiction to favor and scandal; maintain personal integrity to sustain art.
